newsitem.title: GERMANY: Chronology of German minimum reserve changes.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of German minimum reserve changes.

text.p: The following is a chronology of Bundesbank changes to the minimum reserve requirement. The Bundesbank implemented reserve requirements in 1948 and has maintained that this helps it steer monetary policy more deftly.

It is currently the only central bank in an industrialised European nations that requires banks to hold reserves in non-interest bearing accounts. It is also urging the future European Central Bank to use reserves.
December 5, 1996 - The Bundesbank said it would exempt repurchase agreements with maturities of up to one year from minimum reserve requirements from January 1 1997.
August 1, 1995 - The Bundesbank cut resevere requirements on business and sight deposits to two percent from five percent. The requirement on savings deposits was cut to 1.5 percent from two percent.

March 1, 1994 - Minimum reserves on sight deposits between ten million and 100 million marks at domestic institutions were cut to five percent from 9.9 percent and to five percent from 12.1 percent for foreign institutions. Requirements on savings deposits were left unchanged at two percent.
March 1, 1993 - Minimum reserve requirements on savings deposits were reduced to two percent from 4.15 percent. Sight deposits were left unchanged.
